newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Experts urge U.N. convention on corruption.
newsitem.headline: Experts urge U.N. convention on corruption.

text.p: A United Nations panel on corruption meeting in Argentina recommended on Friday the urgent creation of an international convention to stop the globalization of corruption and bribery.

The panel of 10 experts, including former U.S. Attorney General Dick Thornburgh and Russian Accounts Tribunal chief Fyodor Shelyuto, urged U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan to make this a "matter of high priority."

"The international community is in urgent need of a common basis for cooperation that would promote the values of good governance and ensure that development and growth are not impeded by corrupt practices," they said.
The conclusions of a week of brainstorming for the U.N. Committee on Crime Prevention and Penal Justice were set out in a 50-point document of which Reuters obtained a copy.

There were detailed practical tips on legislation for nations troubled by bribery and corruption -- such as host Argentina, where despite years of reforms charges of high-level official corruption are still often front-page news.

Argentine Justice Minister Elias Jassan, vice-president of the U.N. crime commission, faced a grilling on Monday from reporters at the opening of the talks about Argentina's credibility to host such a meeting.

The U.N. panel advised countries to force officials to disclose assets and tax returns, boost independent auditing and set up specialised anti-graft forces such as "general inspectorate, ombudsmen and vigilance committees."
They urged the elimination of bank secrecy to fight money laundering and measures to stop companies or individuals getting tax breaks for bribes to foreign officials.
Such measures could be complimented by laws to forfeit "the fruits of corruption and bribery" and help victims of corruption and extortion recover their funds.
Legislation could also include "aggravating circumstances in cases where corruption is linked with organised criminal actitivies including illicit drug and arms trafficking."

The anti-corruption panel also recommended the U.N. help combat the spread of corrupt business practices across frontiers by "an international convention against corruption and bribery in international commercial transactions."

But as well as stronger legislation, it called for a drive to change public attitudes "to ensure tolerance of corruption is lowered or eliminated" and citizens become aware of their "right to uncorrupted government services."
